new_value:
A forward contract price has an initial value of zero if the value of holding the forward contract (and not holding the asset until some future date) is equivalent to the value of holding the asset now and accruing any costs or benefits of having the asset in the meantime.
If there is a net cost to having the asset now, then the forward price is greater than the spot price, and the net cost is the difference in the forward price and the spot price.
If there is a net benefit to having the asset now, then the forward price is less than the spot price by the value of the net benefit derived from holding the asset.
Forward price = Spot price × (1 + r)^T − Bond coupon payment × (1 + r), where F0 is the forward price today, S0 is the spot price today, C is the bond's coupon payment, T is the time to expiration, and r is the risk-free rate.
In this scenario, the only holding cost is the opportunity cost of capital, which is the risk-free rate of 4%. The benefit of holding the bond is the coupon of 6% that is paid in 1 year. The net benefit of holding the underlying asset is the difference between the bond's 6% coupon and the 4% risk-free rate (ie, 2%).
The bond and bond-forward contract are equivalent positions, so their prices imply the same return until the forward's expiration. For that condition to hold, the forward contract price must be less than the spot price by the net benefit of holding the bond rather than the forward contract (Choices B and C).

Put-call-forward parity describes the relationship between a European call and put option on the same underlying. Each option has the same expiration date and exercise (strike) prices. In put-call-forward parity, each option is a component of separate portfolios. The call option is part of a portfolio known as a fiduciary call, and the put option is part of a protective put:
Fiduciary call: a long position in a European call option on the underlying, and a long position in a zero-coupon bond that matures on the option's expiration date with a face value equal to the option's strike price.
Protective put: a long position in a European put option on the underlying, a long position in a forward contract on the underlying, and a long position in a zero-coupon bond that matures when both the option and forward expire, with a face value equal to the forward price.
Holding a long position in a forward contract and a zero-coupon bond with a face value equal to the forward price replicates owning the stock.
In put-call-forward parity, the payoff is the same for both portfolios when all the derivative instruments expire, regardless of the underlying asset's price at that time. Since the payoffs are identical, the portfolios must have the same value or else an arbitrage opportunity exists.
Using the information in this question, and assuming a discount period of one year, insert the numbers to derive the values of the fiduciary call and protective put portfolios:
The protective put is worth more than the fiduciary call, so there is an arbitrage opportunity (Choice A). To exploit this, the investor would sell the protective put by selling the put option, the forward contract, and the zero-coupon bond, which would result in an inflow of €106. At the same time, the investor would buy the fiduciary call, which would mean buying the call option and the zero-coupon bond, for a net outflow of €105.24. The arbitrage profit is €0.76.

PDF page 6 (8.09, page_idx 5) text is specific to this exact scenario, concludes with the correct answer (Choice B, sell protective put / buy fiduciary call, €0.76 profit). Replaced with the verbatim source explanation.

It is important to understand the difference between put-call parity and put-call-forward parity. Put-call parity implies that a protective put and fiduciary call constructed with options on the same asset and with the same strike price and expiry have the same payoff; therefore, their values are equal at any time prior to maturity.
Put-call-forward parity can be explained based on put-call parity since an investor can create a synthetic equivalent of the underlying asset by going long a forward contract and a risk-free zero-coupon bond whose face value is equal to the asset's forward price. Since it costs nothing to enter a forward contract, the value of the combination at time zero is the zero-coupon bond's present value.
The expression for the synthetic asset position is substituted for S in the put-call parity equation to obtain the put-call-forward parity equation.
In this scenario, to calculate the put option's premium, substitute as follows:
p0 + 45 / (1 + 0.03) = 2 + 50 / (1 + 0.03)
p0 + 43.6893 = 2 + 48.5437
p0 = 50.5437 − 43.6893
p0 = 6.8544, or approximately $6.85.

new_value:
Hedge funds charge a management fee and an incentive fee. The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the total value of the fund's assets under management (AUM). It is assessed each year regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is levied against the fund's annual gains, subject to certain conditions. It is calculated either gross or net of the management fee. The net calculation subtracts the management fee from AUM to arrive at an adjusted AUM that is used to calculate the fund's profits.
The high-water mark represents the value of AUM, net of fees, at any time during the fund's existence. To earn an incentive fee, the fund must exceed the high-water mark, the base from which the fee is calculated.
The hurdle rate is the minimum profit that the fund must earn (usually annually) before it receives an incentive fee. The hurdle rate can either be "soft," meaning that the incentive fee is calculated based on the entire profit, or "hard," meaning that the incentive fee is based on only the excess profit above the hurdle rate.
In this scenario, the fund generated net returns in 20X5 of 18.9% ( = (29.725 – 25) / 25 ), above the soft hurdle rate of 6%, and eclipsed the high-water mark of $27 million. Therefore, the fund earned an incentive fee of 10% of profits, net of the management fee on average assets of $27,500,000:
0.10 × (29,725,000 − 27,000,000) = $272,500.

A hedge fund investor's return is calculated after the hedge fund deducts its fees. Hedge funds typically impose both a management fee and an incentive fee. The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the total value of the fund's assets (ie, assets under management, or AUM). It is assessed at the end of each year regardless of profitability. The fund's management fee is €230 million × 3%, or €6.9 million.
The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits. It can be calculated either after deducting the management fee (net) or before doing so (gross). Also, the incentive fee may be contingent on profits being greater than the hurdle rate and/or AUM being higher than the high-water mark.
This fund has no hurdle rate, but its incentive fee is subject to a high-water mark. In this scenario, the high-water mark of €250 million means that ending AUM must exceed that amount before it can earn an incentive fee from the endowment. With ending AUM of only €230 million, the fund receives no incentive fee.
The endowment's return for the year is calculated as follows (AUM and profits in € millions): adjust AUM after fee deduction (€230 − 6.9 = €223.1), find the fund's profit after fees (€223.1 − 200 = €23.1), then calculate the endowment's percent return net of fees (€23.1 / €200 = 11.6%).
